overview: Nanyue was a powerful kingdom founded by Zhao Tuo around 203 BCE, ruling across parts of today’s southern China and northern Vietnam. Its capital was Panyu, now Guangzhou. The atlas’s 200 to 1 BCE interval continues long after Han conquest in 111 BCE. Its outline also misses Guangzhou, just north of the drawn boundary, so the capital’s archaeological examples below sit outside this imperfect polygon.

periods.title: Kings beside the Han empire
periods.summary: Zhao Tuo built a southern kingdom and accepted Han recognition in 196 BCE; relations involved both negotiation and rivalry.

periods.title: A court recorded in objects
periods.summary: Instruments dated 129 BCE name a royal Music Office; the second king’s tomb preserves evidence of courtly wealth and skilled production.

periods.title: After Han conquest
periods.summary: The royal dynasty ended in 111 BCE. This final part of the imported map interval belongs to subsequent Han rule.

sections.title: Power and the evidence beneath Guangzhou

items.text: Zhao Tuo had served the Qin regime before establishing his own kingdom after its collapse. His realm linked areas now divided between China and Vietnam. Relations with the Han court changed over time: recognition, rivalry and negotiation all mattered. Modern national borders are a poor guide to this ancient political landscape.

In 1983, construction workers at Xianggang in Guangzhou uncovered stone slabs above a royal tomb. Excavators found a seven-chamber burial with a gold seal identifying its occupant as Zhao Mo, Nanyue’s second ruler. The discovery let objects speak alongside the written histories.

The tomb was a major building project beneath a hill. Its red sandstone blocks came from Lianhua Mountain outside Guangzhou rather than simply from the hole being dug. Transporters, stoneworkers and builders were essential to the royal monument, even though their own names do not survive in this account.

Royal luxury had a grim human cost. Fifteen other people were buried as sacrificial victims in the king’s tomb. Their presence is evidence of coercion within this court, not a reason to imagine that every Nanyue family buried its dead in the same way.

sections.title: Food, clothing, health and small comforts

items.text: One bronze roasting stove from the king’s tomb had four little wheels and could be pushed. Its rectangular body was about 61 centimetres long, with slightly raised corners. A movable cooking station was already a practical idea more than two thousand years ago: royal catering had wheels.

Rice, millet and fruit seeds recovered at the palace help reconstruct its food supply. These tiny plant remains complement the impressive serving vessels in the royal tomb. A menu written only from gold and jade would miss the grains and fruit that people actually needed to grow.

A wooden slip excavated at the palace in 2004 identifies “jujube tree No. 94”. This wonderfully ordinary label brings an orchard into the story of a royal court. Even fruit trees could acquire paperwork; keeping track of productive plants was part of managing the palace.

Two small bronze printing plates were found with evidence of matching patterns on silk from the tomb’s western side chamber. Researchers interpret the smaller plate as a guide for alignment and the larger as the main design. Patterned cloth required careful positioning as well as attractive shapes.

Bronze and iron pounding tools accompanied colored mineral substances interpreted as medicines in Zhao Mo’s tomb. The museum connects them with a royal search for longevity. They record attempts to preserve health and life; their burial with the king does not establish that the preparations worked.

The tomb also contained pouring vessels, basins and other water containers. Museum researchers connect these with elite hand-washing rituals shared with the Han court. Keeping hands clean could be part of formal etiquette, with specialized equipment making an everyday action into a ceremony.

A bronze incense burner combined four separate compartments beneath one lid, pierced with diamond-shaped openings. Traces of silk wrapping remained on it. The object shows how carefully designed furnishings could bring scent as well as visual decoration into elite surroundings.

The king’s jade burial suit contained 2,291 plaques, joined or attached using silk and cloth. Its hand and foot coverings used smooth pieces pierced for thread; much of the torso reused pieces cut from older jade or offcuts. Even a spectacular royal burial involved sorting materials and resourceful assembly.

Another gold seal names the Lady of the Right, a court title. Its handle is a small turtle with space underneath for a cord. Such an object preserves a woman’s formal rank within the royal household, although it tells us far less about her thoughts, relationships or daily responsibilities.

Eight bronze goudiao instruments from the tomb carry numbered inscriptions identifying manufacture by the Music Office in Emperor Wen’s ninth year, dated by the museum to 129 BCE. Their graded sizes and numbers connect music with organized workshops and court administration, as well as with performance.

More than 120 iron tools in the royal tomb relate to farming, fishing and handicrafts. Their presence draws attention to the productive work behind courtly wealth. The glittering objects survived beside reminders of people cultivating land, catching food and making things.

Wooden documents recovered from a palace well record official titles, administration, fruit cultivation and hide processing. They show literate workers organizing practical activities, alongside objects associated with ink and writing. This evidence establishes recordkeeping; it does not reveal how many children attended school.

Here is a royal writing sample: 文帝行玺, “Administrative Seal of Emperor Wen”. These are the museum’s modern Chinese character forms for the four characters cut in small seal script on Zhao Mo’s gold seal. The late-second-century BCE object was found on his chest; its dragon handle and imperial wording make authority visible.

sections.title: Water engineering, exchange and the kingdom’s ending

items.text: The royal garden used a large stone-lined pond and an artificial stone brook. Their excavation revealed designed scenery rather than an untouched stream. At another Guangzhou site, a wooden watergate formed part of the city’s flood-control system: managing water served both pleasure and protection.

A silver box from the royal tomb has raised lobes hammered into its body, gilding and an added gilt-bronze foot. The museum relates its technique to West Asian metalworking. It is evidence for connections across long distances, while its exact workshop and journey remain less certain.

Han forces conquered Nanyue in 111 BCE, ending its ruling dynasty. In northern Vietnam, cultural traditions continued under the new imperial order: the national history museum points to bronze drums, pottery and bells with Dong Son features. Political defeat did not make the region’s communities vanish.

ending.text: Han conquest in 111 BCE ended the Nanyue kingdom. The atlas continues its label to 1 BCE, which should be read as a mapping overhang rather than continued royal independence. Communities and local traditions endured within a changed political order.
